-dinosaurs C1.html.description: The briefing — five activities to place your C1 English before the expedition sets out
teaches: The consensus passive: English reports settled findings in the passive and the simple past: the T. rex was considered an apex predator. The agent is left out because the point is the finding, not who found it.
Hedging a claim: Science rarely asserts flatly. Widely believed to have been, is thought to be, appears to have — the hedge marks how firmly the field holds the claim.
The register carries it: A theory gains traction; a discovery transforms our understanding; a habitat is disrupted. At C1 the fixed collocation is the difference between fluent and merely correct.
Third conditional: An unreal past condition takes an unreal past result: if the asteroid had not struck, the dinosaurs would have survived. Both halves have to be in the past.
How sure are you? Swap the modal to change the confidence: would have (certain), might or could have (possible), may have (possible, more formal).
Inversion drops the if: Had the asteroid not struck Earth… is the formal equivalent of if the asteroid had not struck Earth. Invert the auxiliary and the subject, and delete if.
What it does: Having mined the amber block, the player… compresses after the player had mined into three words. It signals that one action finished before the next began.
The subject rule: The participle has no subject of its own, so it borrows the subject of the main clause. Whoever did the first action must be the one doing the second.

b1_prepositions_double_lesson.html.description: Place, time, movement, and the pairs that have to be learned whole
teaches: Inside a space: In means enclosed. A drawer, a box, a room, a pocket — if it has sides and something can sit inside them, it takes in.
On a surface: On means touching a surface. The surface does not have to be flat or horizontal — a wall and a ceiling both take on.
At a point: At marks one specific point rather than an area — an entrance, a desk, a bus stop, the traffic lights.
Two, or more than two: Between needs exactly two clear points — the chemist sits between the two cafés. Among puts you inside a larger, vaguer group of three or more.
Facing it: Opposite means facing something, usually across a street or a room. The two things look at each other.
Out of sight: Behind puts something at the back of something else, often hidden by it — the ball behind the curtain.
Long, medium, exact: In takes the long periods — years, months, seasons. On takes days and dates. At takes clock times.
How long, or since when: For takes a length of time — seven years, two hours. Since takes the point it started from — a date, an event.

b2_prepositions_advanced_lesson.html.description: Purpose, fixed phrases, dependent pairs and the phrasal verbs that carry them
teaches: For + noun or -ing: For names the function of a thing. Boots made for walking, an account for paying fees, a cream for reducing lines.
To + infinitive: To gives the reason a person does something. He saved for a year to buy a van; she she took the early train to avoid the queues.
The test that works: Read what comes after the gap, not who the subject is. For takes a noun or an -ing form; to takes a bare infinitive. That test never fails.
The whole phrase is the word: In terms of, on behalf of, in spite of — these are single items of vocabulary that happen to be three words long. Nothing inside them is chosen.
Bookended by prepositions: Most take one preposition at each end: on the verge of, at the expense of, for the sake of. Drop either and the phrase stops working.
They mark register: This set belongs to formal and written English — reports, speeches, meetings. Using them is part of sounding B2 rather than B1.
Same idea, different preposition: You accuse someone of something but blame someone for it. The meanings are close; the prepositions are not interchangeable.
Three that take a person and a thing: Prevent someone from doing it, congratulate someone on it, succeed in doing it. Each has exactly one preposition.
b2_prepositions_advanced_lesson.html.title: Advanced Prepositions (B2)

b2_prepositions_advanced_lesson_part2.ht.description: The prepositions that carry figures, formal phrases and everyday phrasal verbs
teaches: In, of, by: A rise in demand names what is growing. An increase of twelve percent gives the size. Costs dropping by a fifth gives the size of the change.
From here to there: From X to Y marks the two ends of a change — the fleet grew from nine vans to forty. The starting point comes first.
Comparing and qualifying: Compared to sets two things side by side. A shortage of names what is missing. With regard to narrows to one aspect.
The in family: In charge of, in favour of, in return for, in addition to. Four phrases that all open with in — which is why the first half is rarely the difficult part.
States, not places: Out of the question, under control, beyond doubt. Each describes a condition something is in, and none of them is literal.
The tail is not always of: In charge of, in favour of, but in return for and in addition to. Learning the opening preposition is only half the phrase.
When to is not an infinitive: You object to something, and that to is a preposition — so a verb after it takes -ing. The neighbours objected to the trees being cut down, never to be cut down.
Trusting and mentioning: Rely on someone to do something. Refer to something in a speech or a text. Both fixed, neither negotiable.

carrying-the-load-c1.html.description: What to say to the colleague who does not pull their weight — and what to say next when saying it once does not work
teaches: The claim: An uneven workload rarely announces itself. It accumulates — a deadline absorbed here, a weekend surrendered there, a plan rewritten at midnight because the version that finally arrived was unusable.

What follows from it: Assuming struggle rather than malice is not naivety. It is tactical. A conversation that opens from curiosity gets you an explanation. One that opens from a verdict gets you a defence.

What follows from it: “We agreed the draft would reach me on Tuesday; it came at four on Friday. To hold my own deadline I worked Saturday, and I was frustrated about that. What happened at your end?”

The claim: Often you have done all of that and it went nowhere: a shrug, a counter-example, a list of other people who were also late. That deflection is itself a behaviour, and it takes the same three parts.
What follows from it: “When I raised the delay, you named three colleagues, and we never got to your part. I’m not yet confident this won’t happen again. What will you do differently?”
Rung 1 · Direct feedback: To the colleague, once, calmly. Behaviour, impact, question — and then you stop talking.
Rung 2 · Feedback about the feedback: If rung 1 was deflected, the deflection becomes the behaviour you describe. Same three parts, new subject.
Rung 3 · Bring in your leader: A pattern with dates, what you already tried, and a request for counsel rather than rescue.

escape-from-alcatraz-a2.html.description: Five locked rooms, five pieces of English. Find the numbers, open the last gate.
teaches: Alcatraz was a prison on a small island in San Francisco Bay. It opened in 1934 and closed in 1963. The island is about 1.25 miles (2 km) from the city. People called it The Rock.
In twenty-nine years there were fourteen escape attempts. No prisoner is officially recorded as escaping successfully. The water is cold — about 10–13°C — and the currents are strong.

You are a prisoner in B Block. Tonight you have one night and five rooms: your cell, the corridor, the barber shop, the workshop and the water. In every room you find one number. The five numbers open the last gate.
The rail at the bottom of the screen remembers the numbers for you, so you can think about the English instead. Some rooms have a clock. When you see the clock, look fast.
Use these words to say where something is: in, on, under, behind, next to, between, above. The spoon is under the bed. The vent is behind the sink. The photo is on the wall.
After the preposition comes the and the thing. Never add to. ✓ The light is above the door.✗ The light is above to the door.
One thing: There is. More than one: There are. There is a ladder. There are three pipes.
Questions and negatives keep the same pattern. Is there a guard? — No, there isn’t. Are there any lights? — No, there aren’t.

exam-prep-5hour-course-part2.html.description: Part II: some and any, one and ones, reading technique, and the mock test
teaches: one — singular: I like the red jacket. → I like the red one.
ones — plural: I want the blue shoes. → I want the blue ones.
How to decide: Look back at the noun in the question.

teaches: Reading the stem: Ichno- is a track, osteo- a bone, palyno- pollen, tapho- a burial. The stem names the evidence; -ology just means the study of it.
Why it matters here: Ichnology reads footprints, so it recovers behaviour — herding, speed, hunting — from animals whose bones were never found in that place at all.
The near-miss is the distractor: Phylogenetics reconstructs relatedness, not fossils. In a question about footprints it is plausible, adjacent and wrong — which is exactly what a good distractor is.
The two you know: An ectotherm takes its heat from outside; an endotherm generates its own. Lizard and mammal, roughly.
The one in the middle: A mesotherm generates heat but runs between the two rates. It is how a dinosaur can grow at 600 kg a year without a mammal’s appetite.
The two about stability: Homeothermic means holding a steady temperature; poikilothermic means letting it vary. That is a different question from where the heat comes from.
The number carries the answer: 75% and 95% are not rounding. One is the K-Pg event, the other is the Permian-Triassic. A distractor often differs from the key by a single figure.
Watch the scope word: Exclusively, only, never, confined to — an absolute makes a claim far easier to falsify, and science rarely writes them.

The goal, and the bench: The goalkeeper is the only player allowed to use their hands. The coach (or manager) picks the team and makes the changes from the bench.
Stopped for an offence: A foul is an illegal action on an opponent. A yellow card is a warning; a red card sends the player off for good.
Stopped for offside: A player is offside if they are nearer the opponents’ goal line than both the ball and the second-last defender when the ball is played to them.
Restarting play: Over the touchline → throw-in. Over the goal line off an attacker → goal kick. Off a defender → corner. A foul in the box → penalty.
Nothing conceded: A clean sheet is a match in which your team let in no goals. It is credit to the goalkeeper and the defence together.

forbes-english-ielts-pronunciation.html.description: A quarter of the marks, and the quarter nobody practises: stress, chunking, and the pause that reads as thinking
teaches: Stress marks the meaning: English puts the beat on the words that carry the point and lets the rest run light. Flatten that and every word arrives with equal weight, so the listener has to work out the point unaided.
Six sentences, six words: “I didn’t say she stole the money” means six different things depending on which word takes the beat. The words never change; only the stress does.
The thought group: Fluent English comes in short runs of words said as one unit, with a small break between them. The break is not a hesitation — it is the punctuation of spoken language.

The boundary carries meaning: Move the break and you move the sense. The group boundary is doing the same job a comma does on the page, and putting it in the wrong place misleads the listener in the same way.

Inside a group, keep going: A break inside a group is the one that reads as trouble: pausing in the middle of a noun phrase tells the examiner you have lost the word, not that you are weighing an idea.

Silence is allowed: A short silence at the end of a group reads as thinking. The same length of silence in the middle of a phrase reads as a search for a word. The pause is not the problem — its position is.
Fillers are worse than silence: Errrm and a repeated first word draw attention to the trouble. A clean break does not. If you need a moment, take it quietly — or say that you are taking it.

Talk around the word you lost: If the word will not come, describe what the thing does and keep the turn. Paraphrase is scored under Lexical Resource; stopping dead is scored under Fluency, and not kindly.

forbes-english-ielts-reading-tfng.html.description: The question type that loses the most marks on the Reading paper — and the one that technique, not vocabulary, gets back
teaches: The shape of the paper: Three passages, forty questions, sixty minutes. Roughly twenty minutes each, and the third is usually the hardest — so a passage that runs long is borrowing from the one that needs it most.
The questions follow the text: Most question types run in passage order, this one included. Answer four and you know roughly where the fifth is — you never have to search the whole passage twice.

FALSE: the passage says otherwise: There is a sentence in the text that contradicts the statement. You can put your finger on it. If someone asked you to prove the statement wrong, you would point at that line.
NOT GIVEN: the passage is silent: The text neither says it nor denies it. The statement may well be true out in the world; the passage simply does not go there.
The test is one question: Can I point at the sentence? If yes, the answer is True or False depending on what it says. If you are reasoning — “well, it must be” — the answer is Not Given.
Your knowledge is the trap: A statement can be perfectly true in the world and still Not Given in the text. The examiner is not asking whether it is true. They are asking what this passage says.

TRUE means the text says it: Said in different words, almost always. The passage will not repeat the statement; it will paraphrase it. Matching meaning is the skill — matching words is a habit to break.
Absolutes: All, every, never, only. A passage that says most makes a statement saying all FALSE — the two cannot both hold, and that is a contradiction you can point at.
forbes-english-ielts-reading-tfng.html.title: IELTS Reading: True, False, Not Given

forbes-english-ielts-speaking-part3.html.description: The discussion: answering for people in general, and holding the line when the examiner disagrees
teaches: The person changes: Part 1: “Do you enjoy cooking?” Part 3: “Why do fewer people cook at home now?” The second question is not about your kitchen. Answer for the group.
Three phrases that generalise: Tend to, on the whole, by and large. Each says “this is what is usually true”, and each leaves room for the exceptions the examiner is about to raise.
Your own life still counts: One example, placed after the general claim, shows you mean it. A case in point is… marks it as an illustration rather than as the whole answer.

Pushback is scripted: Examiners are trained to challenge in Part 3, whatever you say. It is not a signal that the answer was weak — it is the part of the test that finds out what you can do under pressure.
Concede, then qualify: Give the other side something true, then keep your ground: That is true up to a point, though… or I would accept that for smaller towns, but…
Changing your mind is allowed: Say it aloud and it reads as thinking: Actually, now that I say it… or On reflection, I would put that differently.
Hedging is vocabulary: Broadly speaking, arguably, in most cases. These are precise words doing a precise job, and precision is what Lexical Resource measures.
Move the claim off yourself: It is often argued that… and There is a case for saying… report a position without signing your name to it, which leaves you free to take it apart a sentence later.

forbes-english-lego-lesson-part2.html.description: Fixed prepositions, idiomatic particles, and the lookalikes that trip B2 learners up
teaches: The same particle, two different jobs: A LEGO set can sell out (no stock left) or be sold off (sold cheap to clear it) — one letter of difference, unrelated meanings.
Idiomatic, not physical: Get round to something has nothing to do with going around anything — it means finally finding the time. The literal image is gone; only the idiom is left.
One verb, two senses: Make out can mean to understand ("make out why") or to discern a shape at a distance. Context decides which.
No other choice: You look forward to something — never forward for, never forward about. The preposition is part of the phrase, not a free slot.
A line, not a scatter: Alongside a street means following its length, in a continuous row. In between means alternating positions. They describe different shapes, not the same idea twice.
Apart from vs take apart: Take apart is the phrasal verb: you take a model apart to sort the pieces. Apart from is a preposition meaning "except for". Neither can stand in for the other.
A particle that does not exist: Sort out means to organise something. There is no sort away, no sort off — swapping the particle does not give you a rarer synonym, it gives you an error.
A verb that needs someone doing it: Run out of needs an active subject: "the store ran out of stock" — not "the stock was run out of". Passive grammar and a phrasal verb do not always combine.

teaches: Active: the subject acts: Subject, verb, object. Lego releases new sets every year. The subject does the releasing, and this is the ordinary way English puts a sentence together.
Passive: the subject receives: Be + past participle. New sets are released every year. The subject is on the receiving end, and the doer can be named with by or left out entirely.
Three steps to turn one into the other: The object becomes the subject; the verb becomes be + past participle in the original tense; the old subject becomes by + agent, and that part is optional.
The simple tenses: Present: Lego makes bricks → bricks are made. Past: they built a castle → a castle was built. Only be moves; the participle never changes.
The perfect tenses: She has tested the set → the set has been tested. He had launched it → it had been launched. The perfect keeps its auxiliary and adds been.
Modals and the infinitive: After a modal, be stays bare: you can assemble it → it can be assembled. The passive infinitive is to be + past participle: designs that might be turned into sets.
When nobody knows who: The brick was dropped. If the doer is unknown, or obvious, or beside the point, the active forces you to invent a subject. The passive lets you leave it out.
When the result is the news: Reports, labels, instructions and science put the thing first: the design was patented in 1958. The patent office is not what the sentence is about.

forbes-english-minecraft-b1.html.description: The tenses a player needs to tell the story, and the words the game gives them
teaches: What you always do: The present simple carries habits and rules: when I find diamonds, I always make armour. It is the tense for what is true every time, not what is happening now.
What has just happened: The present perfect links a finished action to now: I have just found a village. Just means a moment ago, already means sooner than expected, yet means still not.
How long it has been going on: I have been playing for two hours. The activity is still running and the sentence measures it. For takes a length of time; since takes a starting point.
Verbs that only take one noun: You sleep in a bed, not rest in one. You take damage, never make it. You carry a torch, you do not wear it. Each pairing is fixed and has to be learned whole.
Words that describe how often: Diamonds are rare, or uncommon — that is about how seldom they appear. Difficult and hard are about the effort of getting them, which is a different claim.
The connector that warns: Otherwise introduces what happens if you do not: build a shelter, otherwise mobs will attack. Or and or else do the same job in a lower register.
Spawn and respawn: To spawn is to appear in the world — the first time, or after dying. The re- in respawn means again, exactly as it does in rebuild and retry.
Craft, mine, smelt: To craft is to make something with skill from materials. To mine is to dig for stone, coal or iron. To smelt is to heat raw ore in a furnace until it becomes usable metal.

forbes-english-minecraft-c1.html.description: The same game, described by a player and described by a scholar
teaches: The verbs that carry it: A thing constitutes something rather than is it. A region is characterised by its features. A behaviour underpins what follows. A system serves as a channel for something.
The trap: A formal word inside a casual frame is still casual: we do resource acquisition uses the phrase and gets it wrong, because the phrase needs no verb at all.
Prepositions the verb fixes: You adhere to guidelines, and you comply with them — never comply to. Something is regarded as a thing or considered to be one, never viewed for it.

Terms a field has fixed: Content built to rules is procedurally generated. That is the industry’s own term; randomly constructed and computationally rendered describe nothing in particular and would not be understood.
Spawn is intransitive here: Mobs spawn; nobody spawns them. The word describes appearing under conditions, so a transitive use — the game spawns mobs in the sense of creates — misses what it means.

Iterative is not repetitive: An iterative process repeats in order to refine: each cycle improves on the last. Repetitive means the same thing again with no gain, which is the opposite claim about the work.
The abstract nouns: Vigilance is watchfulness maintained against a hazard. A conduit is a channel, usually metaphorical. Cultural resonance is reach and significance beyond the original field.

forbes-english-minecraft-editorial.html.description: Minecraft trivia, and the English that explains how anything turns into anything else
teaches: The change verbs: Lightning transforms a pig into a zombie piglin. It turns into one; it becomes one. Transform and turn both take into, and neither takes to.
Rules prefer the passive: A Charged Creeper is created when lightning strikes. A sponge can only be obtained by defeating an Elder Guardian. The doer is the game, so nobody names it.

Two conditionals for two kinds of rule: Zero for what is always so: if you add a thirteenth block, it doesn’t move. First for what will happen to you: if you attack one, nearby piglins will become hostile.

The noun is never the answer: Every option here names the same kind of thing. What separates them is the clause hung off it: the Gold Pickaxe, despite having the lowest durability. Scan for the clause, not the noun.
Which, who, whose: Which for items and events, who for mobs treated as animate, whose for a property they own: a Charged Creeper, whose explosion radius is doubled.

Concession is the giveaway: Despite, even though, although, but mark the surprising fact, and a trivia question is usually asking for exactly that. Despite takes a noun or an -ing; even though takes a clause.
Say the number exactly: Coordinates go negative: diamonds sit at Y = -58, read minus fifty-eight. Limits are exact: up to 12 blocks, exactly 15 bookshelves.
Compound premodifiers: English packs a whole description in front of the noun and hyphenates it: a gravity-affected block, an iron-tier tool, a 10-block radius, a day/night cycle.

forbes-english-past-modals-minecraft.htm.description: What you should have done, what you could have done, and how you know
teaches: The shape never changes: Every one of these is modal + have + past participle. The modal carries the meaning; have + p.p. only says that we are talking about the past.
Looking back at a mistake: Should have is advice given too late: the right thing did not happen. Could have is the chance that existed and was not taken.
Working out what happened: Must have is near-certainty from evidence. Might have is a guess. Needn’t have says it was done and was not needed.
Almost certain: Must have. There are footprints round the chest, so the thief must have been here. You did not see it; the evidence leaves little room for anything else.
One possibility of several: Might have or could have. Nobody saw who broke the bridge, so it might have been a griefer. It is a guess, offered as a guess.
The negative flips: For a confident negative, English uses can’t have, not mustn’t have: she can’t have finished already.
Should have: You should have built the walls higher. The right action, identified afterwards. It carries criticism, so it lands hard.
Could have: You could have used the Elytra. The ability or the opportunity was there and went unused. No blame attached.

forbes-english-present-perfect-lego-b1.h.description: Two tenses that look the same, and the one question that separates them
teaches: The simple form: Have or has + past participle: she has built the castle. It reports a finished action whose result is still here now.
The continuous form: Have or has been + -ing: she has been building the castle. It reports the activity itself, running up to now.
Both connect past to present: Neither one is a past tense. Both say something about now: the result of the action, or the activity that produced it. Past simple cuts that link.
Counting means simple: Three times, twice, the third time count finished events, and you cannot count an activity that is still running. He has dropped it three times.
Duration means continuous: For two days, all morning, since 2019 measure how long. She has been working on it for two days — the length is the news.
State verbs: Be, have (own), know, like, believe, seem describe states, not activities. A state has no -ing form here, however long it lasts.
Have is two verbs: Owning is a state: How many minifigures have you got? Doing something is not: we have been having trouble with step 12 is fine.
The tired-hands test: When a present state is explained by a recent activity, the state takes the simple and the activity takes the continuous: my hands hurt because I have been sorting pieces.

forbes-geoscience-phrases.html.description: Technical phrases and field expressions used by practising geoscientists — from the wellsite to the seminar room
teaches: Nothing is tested before it is taught: Every phrase in the three activities, and every term in the word bank, is explained on a slide before you meet it in a question. Read the language slides first.
matrix porosity: The intergranular pore space of the rock itself. It usually holds most of the fluid in the reservoir, but it gives that fluid up slowly.
fracture porosity: The void space of a fracture network. It holds very little, but it drains quickly, so the fractures are the main conduits to the wellbore.
structural trapping: Deformation makes the closure: a fold — an anticline — or a fault sealing across the reservoir. The shape of the structure holds the hydrocarbons in.
stratigraphic trapping: A change in the rock makes the closure: a sandstone pinching out, a facies change, an unconformity cutting across the bed. No deformation is needed.
What seals a trap: The cap rock above the reservoir — shale, evaporite or tight carbonate. Its pore throats are fine enough to hold back a buoyant hydrocarbon column.
How a seal fails: A fault offsets it, fractures open a path through it, or the column grows tall enough to force fluid through the pore throats. That last one is capillary leakage.
Immature: Buried too shallow, or too cool for too long. The kerogen has not yet generated hydrocarbons.

forbes-lego-b2-part2.html.description: The prepositions verbs insist on, and four ways to say the same thing better
teaches: Fixed, and not negotiable: A mechanism consists of parts — never from, never in. A fit depends on tolerance, never from. There is no rule underneath these; the verb simply takes one preposition.
Two verbs that look alike: You replace one part with another, but you substitute a new part for the old one. The order reverses, and getting it wrong reverses the sentence.
Phrases that are learned whole: Components go on in sequence, work is done in order, a part is in place. No article, no plural, and no logic to appeal to.
To and too: Too with two os means excessively: too rigid to absorb the impact. To with one is the infinitive marker or a preposition. The sentence usually needs both, one after the other.
Adjectives and adverbs: An adjective describes a thing: an inefficient mechanism. An adverb describes an action: it turned inefficiently. Ask what the word is attached to.
Where errors hide: Both of these survive a read-through because the sentence still makes sense. Proofreading for meaning will not find them; you have to look at what each word is doing.
Too… to…: So stiff that it was impossible to turn becomes too stiff to turn. Nine words become four and nothing is lost. The negative is built in — do not add another.
Only to…: He worked for three hours only to discover a mistake. It marks an outcome that undoes the effort. Not just “and then” — it carries the disappointment.

forbes-lego-b2.html.description: The words engineers actually use, and why the near-synonym is always wrong
teaches: Prototype and blueprint: A blueprint is the plan on paper. A prototype is the first one you actually build, made to be tested and thrown away. One is a drawing, the other is an object.
Modular and iterative: Modular describes the thing: built from self-contained sections you can replace one at a time. Iterative describes the process: build, test, change, build again.
Load-bearing and tolerance: A load-bearing part holds weight the rest depends on. Tolerance is how much error a fit will accept before it stops working — the gap between good enough and not.
Before you start: Lay out the pieces — spread them where you can see them. Cross-reference the diagram with the parts list — check one against the other. Both are preparation, and both are separable.
While you build: Pieces snap into place. When one does not, you troubleshoot the problem — work through it in order until you find the cause.
At the end: You fine-tune the mechanism: small adjustments to something that already works. Not repair, not redesign — the last five per cent.
Read what the word rules out: Align is about position, not connection, so gluing and reinforcing are both wrong however sensible they sound. Each of these words says one thing and excludes the rest.

Orientation is direction, not place: A beam in the wrong orientation is in the right position and facing the wrong way. Wrong length, wrong colour and unattached are three different errors with three different names.

nietzsche-film-vocab-c1-part5.html.description: The vocabulary of film criticism, and the C1 skill of choosing a word by its register rather than its meaning
teaches: Mise-en-scène is not the camera: It is everything composed inside the frame — set, light, costume, where the actors stand. Cinematography is the camera and the lighting technique; blocking is movement alone.

Diegetic means inside the story: A piano playing in the room is diegetic: the characters could hear it. A score is non-diegetic: only the audience can. The line is drawn by who can hear it, not by what it sounds like.

Verisimilitude is not realism: Verisimilitude is seeming true within the conventions of the work. Realism names an artistic movement. Authenticity is a cultural claim; continuity is only consistency between shots.
The distractors are not wrong: At C1 the wrong answer is rarely false. Derivative, imitative, unoriginal and ersatz all say a work copies. Only ersatz accuses it of pretending to be the real thing.

Register follows the document: In a press release a director does not bail out or quit; she withdraws. The informal word is not a smaller version of the formal one — it carries a judgement the formal one refuses.
Praise has a scale too: Memorable is unforgettable. Outstanding is very good. Definitive claims something narrower and larger: the version future performances will be measured against.
Fixed phrases have no logic to appeal to: A studio greenlights a film; nothing else does. Funding arrives at the eleventh hour, never in or on it. These are learned whole or got wrong.
Suffixes carry word class: -al and -ment tend to make nouns, -ive and -ic adjectives, -ly adverbs. Evoke becomes evocative, the way demonstrate becomes demonstrative.

teaches: galvanized · perforated · corroded: Steel dipped in zinc is galvanized, and does not rust. Metal pierced with a field of holes is perforated. Stone or metal eaten away by rain and chemistry has corroded.
inert · dead weight · conduit: Inert means it cannot move itself. Its dead weight is what the structure carries before anybody walks in. A conduit is the tube that keeps cables out of sight.
dilapidated · run-down · vestige: Dilapidated is the strong word: gutters gone, roof open. Run-down is milder and stretches to a whole street. A vestige is what survives of something larger.
conserve · revere · venerate: To conserve is to stop further harm and keep what is there, not to make it new. To revere is to hold in deep respect; to venerate is to do so almost devotionally.
fenestration · articulation: Fenestration is the arrangement of the windows and doors across one face of a building. Articulation is how its parts are jointed and visually separated.

threshold · liminal · promenade: A threshold is the strip you cross at a door — and the level at which something starts to happen. A liminal space is neither one room nor the next: a lobby, a corridor, a stair.

suspended · overarching · trapezoid: Suspended means hung from above. Overarching is literally arching over something, and figuratively the one idea the rest sit under. A trapezoid is a four-sided shape.
pastiche · homage: A pastiche imitates the style of another period or another architect. An homage acknowledges a source while still doing something of its own.

After every preposition, without exception: This is the current on the chart. If a preposition comes first, the verb after it can only be -ing.
As the subject of a sentence: English will not start a sentence with a bare verb, so the verb puts on its noun coat.
After go, for activities: Sports and pastimes you go out and do. Go sailing, go fishing, go shopping, go walking.

After a possessive, in careful English: my, your, his, the captain's. Spoken English usually drops to the object form, and nobody minds.

Asking without asking: The politest way in English to find out someone's plans.
Two futures side by side: Both in progress at the same future time.
Guessing what is going on now: A confident assumption about this very moment.

sherpa-tensing-camp-six-past-continuous..description: Camp three struck the tent and walked away. Camp six goes back and stands inside the day itself — the rain that was already falling, the argument that was…

In the middle of an action in progress: You are standing inside the action, not looking back at it. It had already started, and it had not yet finished.

tense-review-minecraft.html.description: Twelve tenses, thirty questions, and the three decisions that pick between them
teaches: When? Past, present or future. This picks the auxiliary and nothing else: was, is, will be. Every one of the twelve tenses answers this first.
Finished, or still running? The simple form reports a whole event: he built the portal. The continuous shows it in progress and unfinished at that moment: he was building the portal.
Finished before what? The perfect ties one time to another. Had built is finished before a past point; has built before now; will have built before a future point.
What it adds: Have been + -ing takes the perfect’s link between two times and asks how long the activity ran up to the later one. I have been mining all morning counts the morning.
All three times: She has been crafting (up to now), he had been carrying it (up to a past moment), I will have been working nine hours (up to a future moment).
The tell in the sentence: A stretch of time (for three days, all morning, for nine hours) next to a boundary (by the time…, since…) is asking for a perfect continuous.
Finished time blocks the present perfect: Last year, in 2011, yesterday close the time off, and the present perfect needs it open. I have visited the End last year is not English — it is I visited.
Time clauses do not take will: After when, by the time, as soon as, until, English uses a present form for future meaning: when the player enters the Deep Dark…

twin_peaks_prepositions_v5.html.description: What a preposition does to a sentence — not what it means
teaches: 1 · Adverbial: Modifies a verb, an adjective, or the whole sentence. Answers where, when, how, why.
2 · Adjectival: Modifies a noun. Answers which one? Usually called a post-modifier.
3 · Nominal: Acts as a noun itself — subject or object. Rare, and formal.
Place — where? The position of the action. The commonest and the least noticed.
Time — when? how long? Locates the action on a timeline, or measures it.
Direction — where to, where from? Movement with a goal or a source. Contrast this with Place: direction needs a verb of motion.
Manner — how? The way the action is done. Often replaces an adverb.
Reason — why? what for? The cause or the purpose behind the action.
